## Page 1

Deriving SVM. Linear separatable, linear decision boundary, Binary
classification training data.

**goal (output)**

Training data (left) and the trained result (right):

```
 x2│                 x2│        ╱ ╱  h(x)=1
   │ a a       train   │ a a   ╱ ╱ h(x)=w1x1+w2x2+b=0
   │ a a a a  ═════▶   │  a a ╱ ╱ ╱ h(x)=-1
   │ a a               │    ╱ ╱ ╱
   │     b b b         │  ╱ ╱ ╱ b   ▲ margin M
   └─────────── x1     └──────────── x1
                          maximized margine M
```

The SVM.

given any point in plain $(x^*, y^*)$,

$$
h(x^*) = w^\top x^* + b = \left( \sum_{i \in \text{Support Vector}} d_i\, y_i\, \big(X^{(i)}\big)^\top \cdot x^* \right) + b
$$

*[Editorial note: the multiplier is written as a handwritten symbol I read as
$d_i$; it varies a little across the pages (sometimes closer to $\alpha$). It is
the **Lagrange multiplier**, standardly written $\alpha_i$ — which is what the
cleaned note uses.]*

$$
y^* =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{when } h(x^*) > 0 \\
-1, & \text{when } h(x^*) \le 0
\end{cases}
$$

Refresher: unit length of normal vector of the decision line.

$$
\hat{n} = \frac{w}{\lVert w \rVert}
$$

Below is the deriving process. can be skipped if already familiar.

Let ~~$P = (x\dots\,a)$~~ $\;P = (x_1^P,\, x_2^P), \quad Q = (x_1^Q,\, x_2^Q)$

$P, Q$ satisfy:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad & w_1 x_1^P + w_2 x_2^P + b = 0 \\
(2)\quad & w_1 x_1^Q + w_2 x_2^Q + b = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Page 2

The vector $v$ from $P$ to $Q$

$$
v = \begin{bmatrix} x_1^Q - x_1^P \\ x_2^Q - x_2^P \end{bmatrix}
$$

~~$\$$~~ subtract equation (1) from (2)

$$
(w_1 x_1^Q + w_2 x_2^Q + b) - (w_1 x_1^P + w_1 x_1^P + b) = 0
$$

*[Editorial note: the second parenthesis is written $w_1 x_1^P + w_1 x_1^P + b$;
it should read $w_1 x_1^P + w_2 x_2^P + b$. A slip of the pen — the next line uses
the correct terms.]*

So, $\; w_1 (x_1^Q - x_1^P) + w_2 (x_2^Q - x_2^P) = 0$

is equivalent to:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x_1^Q - x_1^P \\ x_2^Q - x_2^P \end{bmatrix} = 0
$$

since the dot product of two vector is $0$, they are perpendicular.

$$
\begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot v = 0
$$

$$
n = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

---

Given a set of $n$ train data points. $\;\big\{\, (x_1^{(i)}, x_2^{(i)}) \mid i = 1, 2, \dots n \,\big\}$

let $m > 0$.

if we enforce:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i = 1, & \quad \text{when } w^\top x^{(i)} + b \ge m \\
y_i = -1, & \quad \text{when } w^\top x^{(i)} + b \le -m
\end{aligned}
$$

we say the decision margin will be $2m$.

we can absorb $m$ into $w$ and $b$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i = 1, & \quad \text{when } \frac{w^\top}{m} x^{(i)} + \frac{b}{m} \ge 1 \\
y_i = -1, & \quad \text{when } \frac{w^\top}{m} x^{(i)} + \frac{b}{m} \le -1
\end{aligned}
$$

now $\dfrac{w^\top}{m}$ becomes $(w^*)^\top$, $\dfrac{b}{m}$ becomes $b^*$.

But we can simplify it and just use $w^\top, b$.

---

## Page 3

Let :

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i = 1, & \quad \text{when } w^\top x^{(i)} + b \ge 1 \\
y_i = -1, & \quad \text{when } w^\top x^{(i)} + b \le -1
\end{aligned}
$$

The margin becomes $\dfrac{2}{\lVert w \rVert}$.

Below we will derive the margin. ( can be skipped if already familiar )

find $x^+$ and $x^-$ from the train data, such that.

$$
w^\top x^+ + b = 1, \quad \text{and} \quad w^\top x^- + b = -1.
$$

To get margin, we just need the vector $x^+ - x^-$ projection scalar on the normal vector.

$$
M = \frac{(x^+ - x^-) \cdot n}{\lVert n \rVert}
= \frac{(x^+ - x^-) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix}}{\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2}}
= \frac{\begin{bmatrix} x_1^+ \\ x_2^+ \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} x_1^- \\ x_2^- \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix}}{\lVert w \rVert}
$$

$$
= \frac{w^\top x^+ - w^\top x^-}{\lVert w \rVert}
= \frac{(1 - b) - (-1 - b)}{\lVert w \rVert}
= \frac{2}{\lVert w \rVert}
$$

So to generate maximized margin $M$, ~~$\dots$~~

We can equivalenty minimize: $\;\dfrac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2$

but still be constrait by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad & y_i = 1, \; \text{for}: \; w^\top x^{(i)} + b \ge 1 \\
(2)\quad & y_i = -1, \; \text{for}: \; w^\top x^{(i)} + b \le -1
\end{aligned}
$$

(1) and (2) can be combine as:

$$
y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) \ge 1
$$

---

## Page 4

We can use `cvxopt.solvers.qp()`, a quadratic programming solver, to solve these
formulas.

In `cvxopt.solvers.qp(P, q, G, h, A, b)` is to minimize $\;\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot x^\top P x + q^\top x,$

Subject to :

$$
\begin{aligned}
G x &\le h \\
A x &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

in our case:

$$
x = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \\ b \end{bmatrix}, \quad
P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
q = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

~~$A =$~~ $A$ an[d] $b$ are not needed.

$$
h = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ \vdots \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \; (n\ \text{rows}), \quad
G = \begin{bmatrix}
-y_1 x_1^{(1)} & -y_1 x_2^{(1)} & -y_1 \\
-y_2 x_1^{(2)} & -y_2 x_2^{(2)} & -y_2 \\
& \cdots & \\
-y_n x_1^{(n)} & -y_n x_2^{(n)} & -y_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

~~$G = [\, x_1\ x_2\ \dots \,]$~~ ~~$+ q =$~~

$$
\left( G = \begin{bmatrix} x_1^{(1)} & x_2^{(1)} & 1 \\ x_1^{(2)} & x_2^{(2)} & 1 \\ x_1^{(n)} & x_2^{(n)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} * y^\top * (-1) \right)
$$

$$
y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) \ge 1 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; -y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) \le -1
$$

---

Now we find solution, from which we can construce SVM.

$$
y^* = \text{class}\left( ~~[\dots]~~ [\, x_1^*\ \ x_2^* \,] \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} + b \right)
$$

---

## Page 5

But the above formula does not directy tell us which data points are support
vectors. How do we find them?

The approach is to reformulat quadratic programming with linear constraints to
~~Lagran~~ Lagrangian formulation.

the quadratic programming:

$$
\underset{w, b}{\text{minimize}}\ \frac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2.
$$

subject to: $\; y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) \ge 1$

$\Longrightarrow$ Lagrangian formulation

$$
\underset{}{\text{minimize}}\ L_p(w, b, d_i) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i \big( y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) - 1 \big)
$$

subject to $\; d_i \ge 0$

So. $\;\dfrac{\partial L_p}{\partial w} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; w = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i\, x^{(i)}.$

$$
\left( \text{for example}: \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 w_1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i \big( y_i (x_1^{(i)}) \big) = w_1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i\, x_1^{(i)} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L_p}{\partial b} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i = 0
$$

Now, calculate the components of $L_p$.

$$
\lVert w \rVert^2 = w^\top \cdot w = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i\, x^{(i)} \right)^\top \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_j\, y_j\, x^{(j)} \right)
$$

$$
= \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i\, \big(x^{(i)}\big)^\top \right) \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_j\, y_j\, x^{(j)} \right)
$$

$$
= \Big( d_1 y_1 (x^{(1)})^\top + d_2 y_2 (x^{(2)})^\top + \dots + d_n y_n (x^{(n)})^\top \Big) \Big( d_1 y_1 x^{(1)} + d_2 y_2 x^{(2)} + \dots + d_n y_n x^{(n)} \Big)
$$

$$
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i\, d_j\, y_i\, y_j\, \big(x^{(i)}\big)^\top \cdot x^{(j)}
$$

---

## Page 6

And.

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i\, w^\top x^{(i)}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_j\, y_j\, x^{(j)} \right)^\top x^{(i)}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i\, d_j\, y_i\, y_j\, \big(x^{(j)}\big)^\top x^{(i)}
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_p(w, b, d_i) &= \frac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i \big( y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) - 1 \big) \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i d_j y_i y_j (x^{(i)})^\top (x^{(j)}) - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i y_i w^\top x^{(i)} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i y_i b + \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i d_j y_i y_j (x^{(i)})^\top (x^{(j)}) - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i d_j y_i y_j (x^{(i)})^\top (x^{(i)}) - 0 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_i d_j y_i y_j (x^{(i)})^\top \cdot x^{(j)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Subject to: $\; d_i \ge 0,\;$ and $\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\, y_i = 0$

---

Recall the $d_i$ was introduced to include conserataints.

$$
y_i (w^\top x^{(i)} + b) \ge 1.
$$

So. $d_i$ should be as large as possible, so that decision is clear.

*[Editorial note: this line is the intuition I want to double-check — see the
"Questions I worked through" section in the cleaned note. Because the dual also
has the $-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum\sum d_i d_j\dots$ penalty term and the constraint
$\sum d_i y_i = 0$, $d_i$ is **not** simply driven "as large as possible."]*

Thus, the Lagrangian Problem is actually:

$$
\underset{d}{\max}\ \underset{w, b}{\min}\ L_p(w, b, d)
$$

This can only be achieved, when ~~$\$$~~ $x^{(i)}$ is support vector, such that
$y_i(w^\top x^{(i)} + b) - 1 = 0$, $d_i$ can be $> 0$.

non support vector, $d_i = 0$.

So: $\; w = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i y_i x_i = \sum_{i \in SV} d_i y_i x^{(i)}$

So, put all things together, we get:

$$
h(x^*) = w^\top x^* + b = \left( \sum_{i \in SV} d_i y_i (x^{(i)})^\top \cdot x^* \right) + b
$$
